subject.title: On a Dead Child
subject.author: Robert Bridges
subject.text:
Perfect little body, without fault or stain on thee,
With promise of strength and manhood full and fair!
Though cold and stark and bare,
The bloom and the charm of life doth awhile remain on thee.

Thy mother's treasure wert thou;-alas! no longer
To visit her heart with wondrous joy; to be
Thy father's pride;-ah, he
Must gather his faith together, and his strength make stronger.

To me, as I move thee now in the last duty,
Dost thou with a turn or gesture anon respond;
Startling my fancy fond
With a chance attitude of the head, a freak of beauty.

Thy hand clasps, as 'twas wont, my finger, and holds it:
But the grasp is the clasp of Death, heartbreaking and stiff;
Yet feels to my hand as if
'Twas still thy will, thy pleasure and trust that enfolds it.

So I lay thee there, thy sunken eyelids closing,-
Go lie thou there in thy coffin, thy last little bed!-
Propping thy wise, sad head,
Thy firm, pale hands across thy chest disposing.

So quiet! doth the change content thee?-Death, whither hath he taken thee?
To a world, do I think, that rights the disaster of this?
The vision of which I miss,
Who weep for the body, and wish but to warm thee and awaken thee?

Ah! little at best can all our hopes avail us
To lift this sorrow, or cheer us, when in the dark,
Unwilling, alone we embark,
And the things we have seen and have known and have heard of, fail us.

title: The Last Duty
standfirst: Robert Bridges' elegy for a dead child, collected in his Shorter Poems of 1890, never lets its speaker call the child their own — “thy mother,” “thy father,” always held at arm's length. Read against the hospital wards Bridges was running at the time, that distance turns out to be the whole poem.

sections.heading: Whoever Is Speaking, It Isn't the Parents
sections.body:
"On a Dead Child" never once lets its speaker claim the child as their own. Look at the second stanza:

> Thy mother's treasure wert thou;-alas! no longer
> To visit her heart with wondrous joy; to be
> Thy father's pride;-ah, he
> Must gather his faith together, and his strength make stronger.

The mother and father are there, named and pitied, but held at a grammatical distance — thy mother, thy father, he, never we or my. Whoever is doing the actual work of the poem is someone else, performing what the third stanza calls, in the period's own phrase for laying out a corpse, "the last duty":

> To me, as I move thee now in the last duty,
> Dost thou with a turn or gesture anon respond;

By the 1870s that phrase belonged to hospital wards as much as to family parlours: laying out a body was a task carried out, not only a private grief undergone. Robert Bridges knew that task from the inside. By the time this poem was [collected into his Shorter Poems](https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.86612/2015.86612.Robert-Bridges-Poetry-And-Prose_djvu.txt), he had already spent several years as a physician on the wards of a children's hospital, and the closest reading of the poem is also the most literal one: this is not a parent's elegy. It is a doctor's.

sections.heading: Five Hundred and Eleven Children
sections.body: Between 5 January 1877 and 11 October 1881, [Great Ormond Street's own record of his career](https://www.hharp.org/library/gosh/doctors/robert-bridges.html) shows Bridges seeing thousands of outpatients and personally admitting 511 children onto the wards of the Hospital for Sick Children — more than half of them for the pulmonary illnesses that killed Victorian children in numbers no antibiotic yet existed to stop. He was doing this work at the same time as a post at the Great Northern Hospital in Holloway. Even the [Royal College of Physicians](https://history.rcp.ac.uk/blog/robert-bridges-poet-laureate-physician) cannot settle which winter he started at Great Ormond Street: one of its own published accounts gives 1878, [another](https://history.rcp.ac.uk/inspiring-physicians/robert-seymour-bridges) gives 1877. What both agree on is the shape of the years that followed — roughly four of them, with laying a dying child back into a hospital bed a fact of his working week rather than a metaphor waiting to be reached for later.

sections.heading: A Household That Had Already Buried Four
sections.body: Bridges was the fourth son and [eighth child](https://history.rcp.ac.uk/inspiring-physicians/robert-seymour-bridges) of John Thomas and Harriett Bridges — a family large even by Victorian standards, and one that, according to [Great Ormond Street's account of its historic medical staff](https://www.hharp.org/library/gosh/doctors/robert-bridges.html), had already lost four children of its own before Robert reached adulthood. The same record notes that he was markedly more conscientious than his colleagues on the wards, giving each child considerably longer than an outpatient clinic seeing well over a hundred cases a day really allowed. A doctor who spends that much time over each patient is a doctor storing something up — not for a case file, in this instance, but for a poem that notices "a chance attitude of the head, a freak of beauty" in a body he is there, professionally, to lay out.

sections.heading: The Pneumonia That Ended It
sections.body: The end came fast, then very slowly. In the summer of 1881, worn lungs and years of casualty-ward hours caught up with Bridges: he came down with a severe case of pneumonia. According to [Great Ormond Street's record of his career](https://www.hharp.org/library/gosh/doctors/robert-bridges.html), what actually kept him from returning to children's wards afterwards was not the illness itself but what it left behind — lapses in memory he no longer trusted around patients. He never went back to full-time practice. Yet the [Royal College of Physicians](https://history.rcp.ac.uk/blog/robert-bridges-poet-laureate-physician) has him remaining, on paper, physician to the Great Northern Hospital until June 1885: four years of a resignation nobody hurried to finalise. The doctor who wrote about laying out someone else's child took the better part of a decade to lay down his own stethoscope.

sections.heading: No World That Rights the Disaster
sections.body:
Every stanza of the poem is built the same way: a long line, two short lines set inside it, a long line again, rhyming around them so the two short lines are quite literally enclosed by the two long ones. Bridges was one of the most exacting metrists of his generation, and it is hard to read six stanzas of a small thing enclosed inside a larger one, in a poem about laying a body into a coffin, as an accident of form rather than an argument made in it.

The last stanza refuses to cash that shape in for comfort:

> Ah! little at best can all our hopes avail us
> To lift this sorrow, or cheer us, when in the dark,
> Unwilling, alone we embark,
> And the things we have seen and have known and have heard of, fail us.

No angels, no better world confirmed, nothing known that survives contact with an actual dead child — from a poet who, [decades later as Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bridges), would write a long philosophical poem called Testament of Beauty arguing for meaning in the universe. Whatever consolation Bridges reached for by the end of his life, at this particular bedside he did not reach for it, and the poem is more honest for the wait.
